analysis.one_liner: Charges fossil fuels a rising emissions fee and sends most of the money back as household rebates.
analysis.headline: Introduced in September 2024 with no cosponsors, the bill sat in the Senate Finance Committee and never received a hearing or vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would put a fee on oil, natural gas, and coal based on the greenhouse gases they release — starting at $65 per ton in 2026 and rising $10 more each year. Most of that money would go back to adults as quarterly rebate payments, with full payments for people making under $75,000 a year ($150,000 for couples). The rest would fund a new Climate Change Finance Corporation making loans and grants for clean energy, transition help for towns that rely on fossil fuel jobs, and payments to farmers who cut emissions.
analysis.who_benefits: Every adult living in the U.S. with a valid Social Security number would get quarterly rebate payments that are not taxed as income and not counted against other benefits; lower- and middle-income households get the full amount, and payments shrink for households above $75,000 single / $150,000 joint. Communities hit by coal, oil, and gas job losses would get transition grants, and farmers would get payments for climate-smart practices.

how_it_helps.text: The bill directs most fee revenue to quarterly rebate payments to every eligible adult, phased out only above $75,000 individual / $150,000 joint income, and paid tax-free and without counting against federal benefits.

It creates a Climate Change Finance Corporation with $7.5 billion a year in initial funding to make grants and loan guarantees for clean energy, vehicle electrification, and climate-resilient infrastructure, with at least 40% of grant funds going to communities facing disproportionate pollution or economic reliance on carbon-intensive industries.

It funds $5 billion a year in transition assistance — job training, early-retirement subsidies, cleanup of coal ash, mines, and abandoned wells — for communities economically reliant on carbon-intensive industries, and creates a separate agricultural program paying farmers for verifiable emissions reductions.

The fee is designed to change behavior over time: if cumulative emissions miss the bill's targets (a 45% cut by 2030 and 100% by 2050 versus 2018), the annual fee increase accelerates from $10 to as much as $25 per ton.

analysis.who_pays: Oil, gas, and coal producers, refiners, and importers would pay the fee, and would pass it into gasoline, heating fuel, and electricity prices — so every energy consumer pays something before rebates arrive. Households above the income thresholds would pay more in fees than they get back, and energy-intensive manufacturers would face higher energy costs and a separate fee on their own process emissions.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil fuel producers and all energy users

drawbacks.text: The fee starts at $65 per ton and rises $10 a year plus inflation, and producers would pass it into fuel and electricity prices, so households would face higher energy bills each quarter before rebate payments arrive.

Rebates phase out at 5% per $1,000 of income above the thresholds, so higher-income households and renters in high-cost areas who file taxes late or not at all could lose money even while paying the fee indirectly.

The bill creates a new independent federal agency with a $7.5 billion-a-year capitalization and broad authority over loans and grants — a large new spending channel whose spending choices would rest with a politically appointed board.

Its border adjustment puts fees on imports of steel, cement, chemicals, and other carbon-intensive goods, which could raise import prices and invite trade disputes, though it also protects U.S. manufacturers from being undercut.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design is deliberately progressive: most fee revenue goes back to households, and the majority of households below the income thresholds would net more in rebates than they pay in higher energy prices. The real costs fall on fossil fuel producers, heavy industry, and higher-income households. The serious risks are transition friction — energy prices rise immediately while rebates take quarters to ramp up — and the scale of the new federal lending agency it would create. The climate payoff is real but long-term and hard for any individual household to see.

outcome.mechanism: Durbin introduced it on September 19, 2024, and the Senate referred it to the Finance Committee, which never acted on it before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Durbin introduced the America's Clean Future Fund Act on September 19, 2024; no other senator cosponsored it.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; that was the final action of record.
The Finance Committee held no hearing, markup, or vote on the bill, and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel producers, refiners, and heavy emitters are better off because the bill never moved: they would have faced a $65-per-ton fee in 2026 rising every year. Ordinary households never got the quarterly rebate payments the bill would have provided, so the status quo — no carbon fee, no rebates — is what remained.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel producers and heavy emitters

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.role: U.S. Senator from Illinois; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in September 2024 and was its only sponsor; no other senator signed on before the Congress ended.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred (chaired by Sen. Ron Wyden, D-OR, in the 118th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill saw no further action.

against.name: The 99 other senators
against.role: No senator besides Durbin cosponsored the bill
against.what_they_did: None of the 99 other senators, of either party, signed on as a cosponsor during the bill's three and a half months of life.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party, so no clear partisan divide ever formed — it simply never gained a second backer before the Congress ended.

industries.industry: Oil, gas, and coal producers, refiners, and importers
industries.note: They would pay the carbon fee directly — starting at $65 per ton of CO2-equivalent in 2026, rising $10 a year — and their customers would see it in fuel prices. Their interest in killing the bill ran against the rebates and cleanup funding ordinary households would have received.

industries.industry: Energy-intensive manufacturers (steel, cement, aluminum, chemicals, glass, paper)
industries.note: They would pay higher energy costs and a separate fee on their own industrial process emissions, but the bill refunds fees on exports, charges equivalent fees on imports of their goods, and pays refunds for captured carbon — shielding them from foreign competition while they adapt.

industries.industry: Clean energy and clean technology industries
industries.note: A new federal finance corporation with $7.5 billion a year in initial funding would issue grants and loan guarantees for solar, wind, geothermal, batteries, EV charging, and carbon capture, creating demand for these industries. Their growth is tied to the emissions reductions the bill aims for.

industries.industry: Banks, credit unions, and green banks
industries.note: The bill guarantees 75% of eligible clean energy loans made by banks, credit unions, and community lenders, and funds state and local green banks — channeling public money through private lenders, who also collect guarantee fees capped by the bill.

industries.industry: Carbon capture, storage, and direct air capture companies
industries.note: Companies that capture and store carbon dioxide get per-ton payments equal to the carbon fee, making capture financially viable; the bill excludes enhanced oil recovery from those payments, limiting the most criticized use.
Farmers would receive payments for verified climate-smart practices and preparation for greenhouse gas credit markets, with extra consideration for underserved and low-income producers.
